{{Short description|Method of generating random small-world graphs}}
{{Network Science}}[[File:Watts-Strogatz small-world model 100nodes.png|thumb|Watts–Strogatz small-world model generated by igraph and visualized by Cytoscape 2.5. 100 nodes.|alt=Watts–Strogatz small-world model]]
The '''Watts–Strogatz model''' is a [[random graph]] generation model that produces graphs with [[small-world network|small-world properties]], including short [[average path length]]s and high [[Clustering coefficient|clustering]]. It was proposed by [[Duncan J. Watts]] and [[Steven Strogatz]] in their article published in 1998 in the [[Nature (journal)|''Nature'']] scientific journal.<ref name=WS>{{Cite journal | last1 = Watts | first1 = D. J. | author-link1 = Duncan J. Watts | last2 = Strogatz | first2 = S. H. | author-link2 = Steven Strogatz | title = Collective dynamics of 'small-world' networks | journal = Nature | volume = 393 | issue = 6684 | pages = 440–442 | doi = 10.1038/30918 | year = 1998 | url = http://worrydream.com/refs/Watts-CollectiveDynamicsOfSmallWorldNetworks.pdf | pmid = 9623998 | bibcode = 1998Natur.393..440W | s2cid = 4429113 | access-date = 2018-05-18 | archive-date = 2020-10-26 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201026170638/http://worrydream.com/refs/Watts-CollectiveDynamicsOfSmallWorldNetworks.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref> The model also became known as the '''(Watts) ''beta'' model''' after Watts used <math>\beta</math> to formulate it in his popular science book ''[[Six Degrees: The Science of a Connected Age|Six Degrees]]''.

==Rationale for the model==
The formal study of [[random graph]]s dates back to the work of [[Paul Erdős]] and [[Alfréd Rényi]].<ref name=Erdos1960>{{cite journal
 | author = Erdos, P.
 | year = 1960
 | title = Publications Mathematicae 6, 290 (1959); P. Erdos, A. Renyi
 | journal = Publ. Math. Inst. Hung. Acad. Sci
 | volume = 5
 | page = 17
}}</ref> The graphs they considered, now known as the classical or [[Erdős–Rényi model|Erdős–Rényi (ER)]] graphs, offer a simple and powerful model with many applications.

However the [[Erdős–Rényi model|ER]] graphs do not have two important properties observed in many real-world networks:
# They do not generate local clustering and [[triadic closure]]s. Instead, because they have a constant, random, and independent probability of two nodes being connected, ER graphs have a low [[clustering coefficient]].
# They do not account for the formation of hubs. Formally, the [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] distribution of ER graphs converges to a [[Poisson distribution]], rather than a [[power law]] observed in many real-world, [[scale-free networks]].<ref name=Ravasz2002>{{cite journal|last1=Ravasz|first1=E.|title=Hierarchical Organization of Modularity in Metabolic Networks|journal=Science|date=30 August 2002|volume=297|issue=5586|pages=1551–1555|doi=10.1126/science.1073374|bibcode=2002Sci...297.1551R|arxiv=cond-mat/0209244|pmid=12202830|s2cid=14452443 }}</ref>

The Watts and Strogatz model was designed as the simplest possible model that addresses the '''first''' of the two limitations. It accounts for clustering while retaining the short average path lengths of the ER model. It does so by interpolating between a randomized structure close to ER graphs and a regular ring [[lattice (group)|lattice]]. Consequently, the model is able to at least partially explain the "small-world" phenomena in a variety of networks, such as the power grid, neural network of [[Caenorhabditis elegans|C. elegans]], networks of movie actors, or fat-metabolism communication in [[budding yeast]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1004264|pmid=26020510|title=Experimental and Computational Analysis of a Large Protein Network That Controls Fat Storage Reveals the Design Principles of a Signaling Network|journal=PLOS Computational Biology|volume=11|issue=5|article-number=e1004264|year=2015|last1=Al-Anzi|first1=Bader|last2=Arpp|first2=Patrick|last3=Gerges|first3=Sherif|last4=Ormerod|first4=Christopher|last5=Olsman|first5=Noah|last6=Zinn|first6=Kai|bibcode=2015PLSCB..11E4264A|pmc=4447291 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Algorithm==
[[Image:Watts strogatz.svg|thumb|Watts–Strogatz graph]]
Given the desired number of nodes <math>N</math>, the mean [[Degree (graph theory)|degree]] <math>K</math> (assumed to be an even integer), and a parameter <math>\beta</math>, all satisfying <math>0 \le \beta \le 1</math> and <math>N\gg K \gg \ln N \gg 1</math>, the model constructs an [[Undirected graph#Undirected graph|undirected graph]] with <math>N</math> nodes and <math>\frac{NK}{2}</math> edges in the following way:

# Construct a regular ring lattice, a graph with <math>N</math> nodes each connected to <math>K</math> neighbors, <math>K/2</math> on each side. That is, if the nodes are labeled  <math>0 \ldots {N-1},</math> there is an edge <math>(i, j)</math> if and only if <math> 0 < |i - j|\ \mathrm{mod}\ \left( N-1-\frac K 2 \right) \leq \frac K 2. </math> 
# For every node <math>i=0,\dots, {N-1}</math> take every edge connecting <math>i</math> to its <math>K/2</math> rightmost neighbors, that is every edge <math>(i, j)</math> such that <math>0 < (j-i) \ \mathrm{mod}\ N \leq K/2</math>, and rewire it with probability <math>\beta</math>. Rewiring is done by replacing <math>(i, j)</math> with <math>(i, k)</math> where <math>k</math> is chosen uniformly at random from all possible nodes while avoiding self-loops (<math>k \ne i</math>) and link duplication (there is no edge <math>(i, {k'})</math> with <math>k' = k</math> at this point in the algorithm).

==Properties==
The underlying lattice structure of the model produces a locally clustered network, while the randomly rewired links dramatically reduce the [[average path length]]s. The algorithm introduces about <math>\beta\frac{NK}{2}</math> of such non-lattice edges. Varying <math>\beta</math> makes it possible to interpolate between a regular lattice (<math>\beta=0</math>) and a structure close to an [[Erdős–Rényi model|Erdős–Rényi random graph]] <math>G(N, p)</math> with <math>p = \frac{K}{N-1}</math> at <math>\beta=1</math>. It does not approach the actual ER model since every node will be connected to at least <math> K / 2 </math> other nodes.

The three properties of interest are the [[average path length]], the [[clustering coefficient]], and the [[degree distribution]].

===Average path length===
For a ring lattice, the average path length<ref name="WS" /> is <math>\ell(0)\approx N/2K\gg 1</math> and scales linearly with the system size. In the [[limiting case (mathematics)|limiting case]] of <math>\beta \rightarrow 1</math>, the graph approaches a random graph with <math>\ell(1)\approx\frac{\ln N}{\ln K}</math>, while not actually converging to it. In the intermediate region <math>0<\beta<1</math>, the average path length falls very rapidly with increasing <math>\beta</math>, quickly approaching its limiting value.

===Clustering coefficient===
For the ring lattice the [[clustering coefficient]]<ref name=AlbertBarabasi>{{cite journal
 | author = Albert, R., Barabási, A.-L.
 | year = 2002
 | title = Statistical mechanics of complex networks
 | arxiv=cond-mat/0106096
 | journal = Reviews of Modern Physics
 | volume = 74
 | issue = 1
 | pages = 47–97 
 | doi = 10.1103/RevModPhys.74.47
| bibcode = 2002RvMP...74...47A
 | s2cid = 60545
 }}</ref> <math>C(0)=\frac{3(K-2)}{4(K-1)}</math>, and so tends to <math>3/4</math> as <math>K</math> grows, independently of the system size.<ref name=Barrat2000/> In the limiting case of <math>\beta \rightarrow 1</math> the clustering coefficient is of the same order as the clustering coefficient for classical random graphs, <math>C=K/(N-1)</math> and is thus inversely proportional to the system size. In the intermediate region the clustering coefficient remains quite close to its value for the regular lattice, and only falls at relatively high <math>\beta</math>. This results in a region where the average path length falls rapidly, but the clustering coefficient does not, explaining the "small-world" phenomenon.

:If we use the Barrat and Weigt<ref name=Barrat2000>{{cite journal
 | author = Barrat, A.
 |author2=Weigt, M.
  | year = 2000
 | title = On the properties of small-world network models
 | journal = European Physical Journal B
 | volume = 13
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 547–560
 | doi = 10.1007/s100510050067
| arxiv = cond-mat/9903411|s2cid=13483229
 }}</ref> measure for clustering <math>C'(\beta)</math> defined as the fraction between the average number of edges between the neighbors of a node and the average number of possible edges between these neighbors, or, alternatively,

:: <math>C'(\beta)\equiv\frac{3\times \text{number of triangles}}{\text{number of connected triples}}</math>

:then we get <math> C'(\beta)\sim C(0)(1-\beta)^3.</math>

===Degree distribution===

The degree distribution in the case of the ring lattice is just a [[Dirac delta function]] centered at <math>K</math>. The degree distribution for a large number of nodes and <math>0<\beta<1</math> can be written as,<ref name=Barrat2000/>

:<math>P(k) \approx \sum_{n=0}^{f(k,K)} {{K/2}\choose{n}} (1-\beta)^n \beta^{K/2-n} \frac{(\beta K/2)^{k-K/2-n}}{(k-K/2-n)!} e^{-\beta K/2},</math>

where <math>k_i</math> is the number of edges that the <math>i^\text{th}</math> node has or its degree. Here  <math>k\geq K/2</math>, and <math>f(k,K)=\min(k-K/2,K/2)</math>. The shape of the degree distribution is similar to that of a random graph and has a pronounced peak at <math>k=K</math> and decays exponentially for large <math>|k-K|</math>. The topology of the network is relatively homogeneous, meaning that all nodes are of similar degree.

==Limitations==
The major limitation of the model is that it produces an unrealistic [[Degree (graph theory)|degree]] distribution. In contrast, real networks are often [[scale-free networks]] inhomogeneous in degree, having hubs and a scale-free degree distribution. Such networks are better described in that respect by the [[preferential attachment]] family of models, such as the [[BA model|Barabási–Albert (BA) model]]. (On the other hand, the Barabási–Albert model fails to produce the high levels of clustering seen in real networks, a shortcoming not shared by the Watts and Strogatz model. Thus, neither the Watts and Strogatz model nor the Barabási–Albert model should be viewed as fully realistic.)

The Watts and Strogatz model also implies a fixed number of nodes and thus cannot be used to model network growth.
